name: Learn: Cluster Hardening
description: Learn node-level CKS cluster hardening step by step on a real multi-node cluster: control-plane manifest file permissions, disabling the kubelet read-only port, the apiserver NodeRestriction admission plugin, least-privilege RBAC, and ServiceAccount token hardening.
objective: CKS › Cluster + System Hardening (15% + 15%). Goal: harden the cluster — manifest file perms, kubelet flags, apiserver admission plugins, and least-privilege RBAC.

questions.title: Harden control-plane file permissions
questions.teach:
Static pod manifests under `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on the control-plane hold sensitive flags (cert paths, tokens, admission config). The kubelet watches that directory and runs each manifest as a *static pod* (its mirror pod shows up in the API named `<pod>-<node>`). CIS benchmarks require these files owned `root:root` with mode `0600` so a non-root user on the node cannot read them.

**File hardening targets CIS asks about (control-plane node):**
- Static pod manifests (`/etc/kubernetes/manifests/*.yaml`): `0600` (CIS allows up to `0644`, but exams usually want `0600`), owner `root:root`.
- kubeconfig files (`admin.conf`, `scheduler.conf`, `controller-manager.conf`): `0600`/`0644`, `root:root`.
- PKI: `/etc/kubernetes/pki/*.crt` → `0644`, but **private keys** `*.key` → `0600`.
- etcd data dir (`/var/lib/etcd`): `0700`.

**Tools:** `chmod <mode> <file>` sets the mode; `chown root:root <file>` sets ownership; verify with `stat -c '%a %U:%G' <file>`.

**Gotchas:**
- Changing a manifest's **mode/owner does NOT restart its pod** (safe to do live). Changing the file's *contents* does restart the static pod.
- Don't confuse the numeric mode `600` (`rw-------`) with `644` (`rw-r--r--`). `stat -c '%a'` prints the octal; `ls -l` prints the symbolic form.
- On a kind cluster each node is a container, so you reach the node with `docker exec <node>` (on a real exam you'd `ssh` to the node).
- Private keys need `0600`; public certs can stay `0644` — don't blanket-chmod a whole directory.
questions.prompt:
The kube-scheduler static pod manifest on control-plane node `$CP` was left world/group readable at mode `644`. Set `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` on `$CP` to exactly mode `600`.

Target: `docker exec $CP stat -c '%a' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` prints `600`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml   # 600 root:root

questions.title: Disable the kubelet read-only port
questions.teach:
The kubelet can serve an **unauthenticated, read-only port** (`10255`) that leaks pod and node metadata (`/pods`, `/metrics`, `/stats`) to anyone who can reach it — no auth, no TLS. CIS requires it disabled by setting `readOnlyPort: 0` in the kubelet config. The *authenticated* serving port `10250` stays up for the API to talk to; only `10255` is the leak.

**Where kubelet settings live (two mechanisms):**
- **Config file** (preferred, `KubeletConfiguration` object): usually `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`. Set `readOnlyPort: 0` here. The path is pointed to by `--config` in the kubelet's systemd drop-in (`/var/lib/kubelet/kubeadm-flags.env` / `/etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/`).
- **Command-line flags** on the kubelet process (e.g. `--read-only-port=0`). Flags override the config file. Check the actual running process with `ps aux | grep kubelet` to see which is in effect.

**Other kubelet hardening CIS/CKS cares about (same file):**
- `authentication.anonymous.enabled: false` (reject anonymous requests on `10250`).
- `authorization.mode: Webhook` (not `AlwaysAllow`).
- `authentication.x509.clientCAFile` set (require client certs).
- `protectKernelDefaults: true`, `--make-iptables-util-chains`.

**Gotchas:**
- Config changes need a **`systemctl restart kubelet`** to take effect — editing the file alone does nothing.
- After the restart the node briefly goes `NotReady`; wait ~20s and confirm `kubectl get node <node>` shows `Ready` again. A typo in the YAML can make the kubelet fail to start — check `systemctl status kubelet` / `journalctl -u kubelet`.
- If a `--read-only-port` flag is also set on the command line, setting `readOnlyPort: 0` in the config won't help — the flag wins.
- `readOnlyPort: 0` means *disabled*; any non-zero value enables it.
questions.prompt:
On worker `$W1` the kubelet is serving its read-only port (seeded as `readOnlyPort: 10255`). Edit `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` on `$W1` so that `readOnlyPort: 0`, then restart the kubelet. Give the node ~20s to report `Ready` again.

Target: the config on `$W1` has `readOnlyPort: 0` AND node `$W1` is `Ready`.
questions.hint: `docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, then `docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
docker exec $W1 grep readOnlyPort /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   # readOnlyPort: 0
docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W1   # wait ~20s for Ready

verification.description: node $W1 is still Ready after the kubelet restart

questions.title: Re-enable the NodeRestriction admission plugin
questions.teach:
`NodeRestriction` is an API-server **admission controller** that limits what each kubelet (identity `system:node:<name>` in group `system:nodes`) can modify to **only its own Node object and the Pods bound to it** — so a compromised node cannot tamper with other nodes, read arbitrary Secrets, or escalate. It's one layer of a defense-in-depth story alongside the `Node` authorizer.

**How admission plugins are configured on kube-apiserver (static pod manifest `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml`):**
- `--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,...` — comma-separated list to turn ON (in addition to the defaults). Append `,NodeRestriction` to an existing value; don't drop the others.
- `--disable-admission-plugins=...` — turn OFF default-on plugins.
- `--admission-control-config-file=...` — for plugins needing config (e.g. `PodSecurity`, `ImagePolicyWebhook`, `EventRateLimit`).
- Many plugins are **on by default** in the apiserver (e.g. `ServiceAccount`, `PodSecurity`, `ResourceQuota`); `NodeRestriction` isn't an apiserver default but **kubeadm** enables it. You don't list those to keep them, only to re-add if removed.

**Other security-relevant admission plugins (CKS):** `PodSecurity` (Pod Security Admission), `ImagePolicyWebhook`, `AlwaysPullImages`, `EventRateLimit`, `ValidatingAdmissionWebhook`/`MutatingAdmissionWebhook`.

**Gotchas:**
- Editing the apiserver manifest makes the kubelet **restart the apiserver automatically** — a typo (bad YAML/indent, duplicate flag) takes the apiserver DOWN and `kubectl` stops responding. Keep a backup copy of the file before editing.
- After saving, wait ~20–60s and poll `kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP`; the mirror pod gets recreated.
- Flag value is a single comma-separated string — don't add a second `--enable-admission-plugins` line (last one wins / may error); merge into one.
- Check the actually-running flags with `kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep admission`, not just the file on disk.
questions.prompt:
Setup removed `NodeRestriction` from the apiserver's `--enable-admission-plugins`. Edit `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` on `$CP` so the flag includes `NodeRestriction` again (keep any other plugins), then wait for the apiserver to come back.

Target: the running kube-apiserver has `NodeRestriction` in `--enable-admission-plugins`.
questions.hint: `docker exec -it $CP bash`, then add the line `- --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction` under the kube-apiserver command args (or append `,NodeRestriction` to an existing value). Save and wait ~20s for the apiserver to restart.
questions.solution:
# Setup removed the flag line, so add it back under the kube-apiserver args:
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# (If the flag already exists with other plugins, instead append ,NodeRestriction to its value.)
# Wait ~20s for the apiserver to restart, then verify:
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins

questions.title: Least-privilege RBAC for a workload
questions.teach:
Workloads should get the **minimum** API access they need. Grant a ServiceAccount a narrow **Role** (only the verbs/resources required) via a **RoleBinding** — never `cluster-admin`.

**The four RBAC objects:**
- **Role** — namespaced permissions. **ClusterRole** — cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs), *or* reusable namespaced rules, *or* non-resource URLs (`/healthz`).
- **RoleBinding** — grants a Role (or a ClusterRole) *within one namespace*. **ClusterRoleBinding** — grants a ClusterRole cluster-wide (all namespaces).
- Key trick: a **RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole**, scoping those cluster-wide rules down to just its namespace (common for reusing `view`/`edit`).

**Rule fields:** `apiGroups` (`""` = core group for pods/services/configmaps), `resources` (plural, e.g. `pods`, `pods/log`, `deployments`), `verbs` (`get,list,watch,create,update,patch,delete,deletecollection`), and optional `resourceNames` to pin specific objects.

**Subjects:** `kind: User`, `kind: Group`, or `kind: ServiceAccount` (an SA's RBAC name is `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>`, group `system:serviceaccounts`).

**Verify effective access** without logging in: `kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name> -n <ns>` → the SA should do exactly what you granted and nothing more. `--list` dumps all perms.

**Gotchas:**
- `resourceNames` **cannot restrict `list`, `watch`, or `create`** (the name isn't known at request time for those) — only get/update/patch/delete.
- Imperative shortcuts: `kubectl create role`, `kubectl create rolebinding --role=/--clusterrole= --serviceaccount=<ns>:<name>`. `--serviceaccount` takes `ns:name`, not just the name.
- A RoleBinding's `roleRef` is **immutable** — to change which role it points to, delete and recreate.
- `watch` and `list` are separate verbs; a client that watches usually needs both. Subresources (`pods/exec`, `pods/log`) must be listed explicitly.
- RBAC is purely additive (deny by default); there are no deny rules.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-learn` a ServiceAccount `reader` already exists. Create a Role granting only `get,list` on `pods` and a RoleBinding binding it to that SA.

Target: SA `reader` can `list pods` (`yes`) but cannot `delete pods` (`no`) in `cks-learn`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n cks-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods`, then `kubectl -n cks-learn create rolebinding reader-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=cks-learn:reader`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n cks-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods
kubectl -n cks-learn create rolebinding reader-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=cks-learn:reader
kubectl auth can-i list pods   --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # no

verification.description: SA reader can list pods but cannot delete pods in cks-learn

questions.title: ServiceAccount token hardening
questions.teach:
By default every pod mounts a ServiceAccount token at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/` (via a **projected volume**: `token`, `ca.crt`, `namespace`). Handy for calling the API, but if the pod is compromised the token is stolen. Pods that never call the API should not mount one.

**Disabling the automount — two places:**
- On the **ServiceAccount**: `automountServiceAccountToken: false` (top-level field, not under `spec`). Applies to every pod using that SA.
- On the **pod spec**: `spec.automountServiceAccountToken: false`. The **pod-level setting overrides the SA-level** setting when both are present.
- With it off, no `kube-api-access-*` projected volume/mount is added to the container.

**Related token facts (CKS):**
- Modern tokens are **short-lived, audience-bound, auto-rotated** projected tokens (TokenRequest API) — not the old forever Secret.
- You can still mint a token manually: `kubectl create token <sa> --duration=...`.
- A long-lived token Secret only exists if you explicitly create a `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` Secret annotated `kubernetes.io/service-account.name`.
- Every namespace has a `default` SA; pods with no `serviceAccountName` use it — lock that down too.

**Gotchas:**
- `automountServiceAccountToken` on the SA sits at the **top level** of the object, *not* inside a `spec:` block — a common YAML mistake.
- Set `serviceAccountName` (the field is `serviceAccountName`, the deprecated alias `serviceAccount` still appears in dumps) on the pod, or it falls back to `default`.
- Even with the token mounted, access is still gated by RBAC — but defense in depth says don't mount what you don't need.
- Changing the SA setting does **not** affect already-running pods; the token is bound at pod creation, so recreate the pod.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-learn`, create a ServiceAccount `no-token` with `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, then run a pod `hardened` using that ServiceAccount (image `busybox:1.36`, e.g. `sleep 3600`).

Target: SA `no-token` has `automountServiceAccountToken: false` AND pod `hardened` runs as SA `no-token` with no SA token volume mounted.
questions.hint: Create the SA, patch/set `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, then create the pod with `serviceAccountName: no-token`. Apply a manifest with `kubectl apply -f -`.
questions.solution:
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: no-token
  namespace: cks-learn
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hardened
  namespace: cks-learn
spec:
  serviceAccountName: no-token
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
YAML

verification.description: SA no-token has automount disabled and pod hardened uses it with no token mounted
